newsitem.title: ITALY: Berlusconi party backs Italian reform commission.
newsitem.headline: Berlusconi party backs Italian reform commission.

text.p: Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Forza Italia party has agreed to back government plans to set up a bicameral parliamentary commission to work out changes to Italy's outdated 1948 constitution.
The decision was taken late on Monday after a four hour meeting of Forza Italia politicians.
"The battles (over reform) will be done in the commission," Forza Italia parliamentarian Giuliano Urbani said.
"It certainly won't be a walk in the park because we have to rebuild the state. However, at least we will lift the political debate to a higher level," he told reporters.
Berlusconi is due to meet his allies in the centre-right Freedom Alliance opposition bloc later on Tuesday to try to persuade them to back the bicameral proposals.

Hard-right leader Gianfranco Fini said recently he wanted to vote against the commission in the Senate (upper house) on Wednesday and force a referendum in favour of creating a separate, newly elected assembly to tackle the reforms.
Before Monday's meeting, a number of Forza Italia politicians indicated that they would prefer to see a constituent assembly formed.
Both houses of parliament voted in favour of a bicameral commission last summer but must do so a second time before the 70-member body can begin work.

The Senate vote will be followed by a vote in Chamber of Deputies on January 21. Change requires a two-thirds majority of members of parliament. Commentators said Forza Italia's support should be enough to secure this majority.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has firmly rejected calls for a separate assembly, arguing that the bicameral commission was the only body capable of initiating reforms quickly enough.
Italian politicians have been discussing reforms to their post-World War Two constitution for 15 years but without real progress.

Many commentators hoped the huge corruption scandals that felled the old ruling elite in the early 1990s would bring swift reform but little has been done. Prodi's government, the 55th since the war, says it has an historic duty to achieve reform.
